text: Welcome to Hybrid Quantum-Classical Computing. This first lesson makes one argument and backs it with evidence: there is no such thing as a quantum program that runs start to finish on a QPU alone. Every real quantum application is a classical program that calls out to quantum hardware for a few specific operations, and does everything else on ordinary CPUs.

A QPU is good at exactly three things today: preparing and evolving entangled states for a narrow set of problems, evaluating a cost function encoded in a quantum observable, and generating samples from distributions that are hard to sample classically. Everything else — reading data, deciding what circuit to run next, aggregating results, handling an outage, tracking spend — is ordinary software engineering. In a typical hybrid application, over ninety-five percent of the code you write never touches a QPU.

Here's what that looks like in a real console. This is Amazon Braket's Service Dashboard — notebooks, hybrid jobs, announcements, community links. Almost none of it is the quantum hardware itself. It's the classical tooling that surrounds it.

And here's the hardware: Braket's Devices page. IonQ, IQM, QuEra, Rigetti — nine devices total, each just a remote endpoint with a status. A QPU, as every current cloud provider exposes it, can't load a file, branch on a condition, or decide what to run next. It accepts a fixed circuit, executes it some number of times, and returns measurement counts. Nothing more.

This is the entire scope of what one of those devices actually runs — a real two-qubit circuit from IBM Quantum's own documentation. A Hadamard gate, a controlled-X gate, a measurement. That's it. Deciding what circuit this should be, and what to do with the answer, is entirely classical work.

So here's the diagram you'll draw constantly in this course. On one side, a classical control loop: data prep, an optimizer step, a convergence check, cost tracking — code you own completely. It submits a circuit to a quantum cloud API and gets measurement counts back. That's the whole interface. The box on the left is where a hybrid engineer spends almost all their time; the box on the right is a black box you call over a network connection.

Treat the classical control loop as the application, with the QPU as one expensive, occasionally-unreliable remote dependency it calls, and your priorities fall into the right order. That's the framing this entire course is built around. Next lesson, we turn it into a concrete, step-by-step loop: the variational hybrid pattern behind VQE, QAOA, and variational classifiers.
